content.intro: This lesson covers Image Promotion Between Environments. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Treat image promotion between environments as a behavior to explain and verify, not a command to memorize. Identify the Docker component or setting involved, predict the outcome, then confirm it using a small isolated lab and a recorded result. Learning image promotion between environments helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for image promotion between environments. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Image Promotion Between Environments
content_blocks.code:
docker image ls
# After authenticating to an authorized test registry:
# docker image tag LOCAL_IMAGE:VERSION REGISTRY/OWNER/IMAGE:VERSION
# docker push REGISTRY/OWNER/IMAGE:VERSION
content_blocks.expected_output: The first command lists local images. The commented commands show the tag/push pattern without inventing a registry name or publishing anything.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use `docker login` only with your own authorized account or token and a disposable repository. Replace every uppercase placeholder before a push.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No reset for image listing. If you pushed a test tag, delete it later according to your registry retention policy.
content_blocks.safety_note: The upload commands are comments. Do not publish a private, vulnerable, or unreviewed image.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
